output.title: When scope starts to wander, draw the box first
output.body:
If you want to spot early signs of unbounded scope, watch for the moment a single workflow turns into a wish list. That usually happens when the owner starts from a broad business goal instead of one repeatable job. The useful question is not “Can AI help the business?” It is “What is the one recurring workflow we can actually describe from input to output?”

Start with the clearest repeatable item: invoices processed, leads responded to, or data transferred. Then write the boundary in plain English. What goes in, what decision is made, what comes out, and what is explicitly out of scope. For example, “respond to customer emails” is a workflow. “Improve customer satisfaction” is a business ambition. Important, but not the same thing. The box has to stay a box; otherwise the project quietly becomes a small universe.

A practical next step is to test fit with three questions: are the decisions mostly rule-based, is there enough past example data to show the pattern, and can a wrong answer be caught before it reaches the customer? If all three are yes, you probably have a bounded pilot. If not, the scope likely needs restructuring, or the job may be better handled by a person. For payments or other high-risk actions, human approval stays in the loop.
